• OTP verification requires matching parameters on both sides, including the shared secret, hash, time interval, and code length. Clock differences can cause a code to be rejected.
  • The generated OTP is associated with the selected timestamp and interval; use Set now when generating a code for the current time.
  • Treat the shared key as sensitive. The generation details, including the key and OTP, are also written to BerEditor's log.
  • Clear Data All clears the key and result values. It does not change the selected time or OTP parameters.

docs.title: Get BER from URI Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Get BER from URI dialog retrieves BER-encoded data from an HTTP(S) or LDAP address and loads the result into the main BerEditor window for decoding. Open it from Tool > Get BER from URI.

Figure 1. Get BER from URI dialog. Enter an HTTP(S) or LDAP address, or enable LDAP Host Information to supply LDAP connection and search details separately.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. URI Address — Enter or select an address. Recent addresses are available from the drop-down list. The dialog accepts http, https, and ldap schemes.
  2. Example — Shows an example certificate URL.
  3. Clear Used URI — Removes the saved recent URI list.
  4. Use LDAP Host Information — Switches from a full URI to separately entered LDAP connection details. When enabled, the URI field is disabled and the LDAP Host Information group is enabled.
  5. LDAP Host Information — Enter the LDAP server Host, Port, and search DN. The host and port are retained as settings for later use.
  6. LDAP Search Condition — Supplies LDAP search options: Scope, certificate Type, and Filter. The default filter is (objectClass=*).
  7. Get — Retrieves data from the selected address and asks BerEditor to decode the returned data.
  8. Close — Closes the dialog.

docs.title: Retrieve Data from an HTTP(S) URI
docs.text:
1. Leave Use LDAP Host Information unchecked.
  2. Enter or select an http:// or https:// address in URI Address.
  3. Select Get.
  4. If retrieval succeeds, BerEditor decodes the returned data in the main window and displays a success message.

The address can also be selected from the recent URI list. Successfully used addresses are saved in that list. Clear Used URI removes the saved list.

docs.title: Retrieve Data from LDAP
docs.text: You can provide LDAP details in either of these ways:

docs.title: Use an LDAP URI
docs.text:
1. Leave Use LDAP Host Information unchecked.
  2. Enter an ldap:// URI that identifies the LDAP server and search location.
  3. Set the search Type and Filter if needed.
  4. Select Get.

The dialog reads the server, DN, scope, filter, and requested attribute from the LDAP URI when those values are present. The selected Type and filter field are used as defaults where the URI does not specify them.

docs.title: Enter LDAP Host Information Separately
docs.text:
1. Select Use LDAP Host Information.
  2. Enter the LDAP server Host, Port, and DN.
  3. Choose a Scope, Type, and Filter.
  4. Select Get.

The current implementation provides the BASE scope. Available certificate types are caCertificate, signCertificate, userCertificate, certificateRevocationList, autorithRevocationList, deltaRevocationList, and certificateTrustList.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Enter an address before selecting Get. The dialog reports an error when the URI is empty or uses an unsupported scheme.
  • For LDAP host mode, provide a DN. Check the host, port, and server availability if connection or bind errors appear.
  • If retrieval fails, BerEditor reports the retrieval error in a warning or log message.
  • Retrieved data is passed to the main BER decoder. If the server returns data that is not valid BER, decoding may fail even when the network request succeeds.

docs.title: Key Agreement Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Key Agreement dialog calculates a shared secret using Diffie–Hellman (DH) or Elliptic Curve Diffie–Hellman (ECDH). It can also generate the parameters and key material used in the calculation.

Figure 1. Key Agreement dialog with the DH tab selected. The ECDH tab provides equivalent key agreement controls for elliptic-curve keys.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. DH / ECDH tabs — Select finite-field DH or elliptic-curve ECDH.
  2. DH parameters — In the DH tab, choose Parameter Len, select the g value (generator), and enter the p value (prime modulus) as hexadecimal. GenParam generates DH parameters. Import and Export load and save DH parameters.
  3. A and B keys — Enter each participant's private and public keys in hexadecimal. Use GenPriKey to generate a private key and GenKeyPair to generate a key pair. The public key is derived from the corresponding private key and DH/ECDH parameters.
  4. ECDH parameters and key tools — In the ECDH tab, choose a curve or parameter set. The adjacent field displays its identifier. The A and B key areas provide controls to generate or check keys, find a private-key file, or retrieve keys from CertMan or KeyPairMan.
  5. Edit Mode — Enables editing of all A/B private and public key fields. In calculation mode, only the fields needed for the selected participant are enabled.
  6. A Calculate / B Calculate — Select which participant computes the shared secret. Run performs that calculation.
  7. Display shared key Y value — For ECDH, also display the Y component of the computed shared point when available. The shared secret's X component is shown by default.
  8. Secret Key — Displays the calculated result in hexadecimal and its length. C clears this output.
  9. Clear Data All / Close — Clear the dialog's values or close the dialog.

docs.title: Calculate a DH Shared Secret
docs.text:
1. Select the DH tab.
  2. Choose a parameter length and generator, or enter/import the agreed p and g values. Both participants must use the same parameters.
  3. Enter or generate A's and B's private/public keys. For A's calculation, provide A PrivateKey and B PublicKey. For B's calculation, provide B PrivateKey and A PublicKey.
  4. Select A Calculate or B Calculate, then select Run.
  5. Read the resulting shared value in Secret Key. The dialog also writes calculation details to BerEditor's log.

docs.title: Calculate an ECDH Shared Secret
docs.text:
1. Select the ECDH tab and choose the same curve or parameter set used by both participants.
  2. Enter or generate the participant key pairs. To calculate as A, provide A PrivateKey and B PublicKey; to calculate as B, provide B PrivateKey and A PublicKey.
  3. Select the calculation side and choose Run.
  4. Read the shared secret in Secret Key. Enable Display shared key Y value if you also need the Y component shown.

docs.title: Generate and Import Parameters or Keys
docs.text:
• In the DH tab, select a parameter length and use GenParam to create parameters. Use Export to save them or Import to load existing parameters.
  • Use GenPriKey and GenKeyPair to create DH key material. The private key and public key must belong to the same participant and parameters.
  • In the ECDH tab, select the desired curve before generating keys. The FindPriKey, GetFromCertMan, and GetFromKeyPair controls can load existing private/public key material. The check controls validate the displayed public key or key pair.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A and B must use the same DH parameters or ECDH curve, and each side must calculate with its own private key and the other side's public key. Both calculations should produce the same shared secret.
  • Values entered directly in the key and parameter fields use hexadecimal encoding.
  • Edit Mode is useful when preparing both participants' values manually; the normal A/B calculation selection enables the inputs required for that calculation.
  • Treat private keys and shared secrets as sensitive data. Clear the fields when finished if the dialog should not retain them.

docs.title: KeyList Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Symmetric Key List dialog stores and selects symmetric keys used by BerEditor's encryption, decryption, and MAC tools. The list displays each key's name, algorithm, length, IV availability, and last-modified time.

Figure 1. Key List in management mode. Select a row to view, delete, or use the stored key.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Save Path — Shows the configured key-list storage folder. The adjacent filter shows All keys or narrows the list by algorithm, including generic keys and HMAC keys.
  2. Key table — Lists stored keys with Name, Algorithm, Len, IV, and LastModified columns. IV indicates whether an initialization vector is associated with the entry. Select a row before using an action.
  3. Key View — Opens the selected key entry for inspection.
  4. Key Add — Opens the key editor to create a named key entry. Enter its algorithm, key value, and optional IV.
  5. Key Delete — Removes the selected key entry from the configured key-list folder.
  6. Gen MAC — Opens the MAC generator using the selected key.
  7. Encrypt/Decrypt — Opens the symmetric encryption/decryption tool using the selected key.
  8. OK / Close — In selection mode, OK returns the selected key (and associated IV where applicable) to the calling dialog. Close dismisses the key list.

docs.title: Add or Inspect a Key
docs.text:
1. Select Key Add and enter a unique key name, algorithm, key value, and optional IV in the key editor.
  2. Save the entry. It appears in the table with its algorithm, length, IV indicator, and modification time.
  3. Select a row and choose Key View to inspect the stored entry. In management mode, right-click a row for the view and delete actions.

docs.title: Select a Key for Another Tool
docs.text:
1. Open KeyList from the dialog that needs a symmetric key.
  2. Optionally filter by algorithm, then select the desired key row.
  3. Select OK or double-click the row to return the key to the calling dialog.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• A key entry's name must be unique within the configured key-list folder.
  • The key list supports algorithm-specific and generic key entries, as well as HMAC keys. The caller may filter the list to a specific algorithm.
  • Treat stored symmetric keys and IV values as sensitive. Deleting an entry removes its file from the key-list folder.

docs.title: Key Management Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Key Management dialog provides three tools: key derivation, symmetric key wrapping/unwrapping, and key encapsulation. Open it from Cryptography > Key Manage.

Figure 1. Key Management dialog on the KeyDerive tab. The dialog also contains KeyWrap and KEM tabs.

docs.title: Tabs
docs.text: Tab Purpose KeyDerive Derives a key using PBKDF2, HKDF, ANS X9.63, or Scrypt. KeyWrap Wraps or unwraps key bytes using KW or KWP and a key-encryption key (KEK). KEM Encapsulates a shared key using a public key or decapsulates it using the matching private key.

docs.title: Key Derivation
docs.text:
1. Open KeyDerive and select a derivation method.
  2. Enter the password or secret and choose its input representation where available.
  3. Enter method-specific salt and information values, and select a hash where applicable.
  4. Set the desired Derived Key Len in bytes and any method parameters.
  5. Select Derive Key. The derived key is displayed as hexadecimal.
Method Main inputs PBKDF2 Password (String), salt, iteration count, hash, and key length. HKDF Secret, salt, optional Info, hash, and key length. A salt is required by this dialog. ANS.X963 Secret, Info, hash, and key length. Scrypt Password, salt, N/r/p parameters, and key length. The hash and Info controls are not used.

The input type selectors for secret, salt, and Info use the available data formats shown by the dialog, such as Hex, String, and Base64. Length fields are calculated automatically. Use the salt C button or the derived-key C button to clear those fields. Clear Data All clears the dialog's derivation, wrapping, and KEM data.

docs.title: Key Wrap and Unwrap
docs.text:
1. Open KeyWrap and choose KW or KWP under Method.
  2. Choose Wrap or Unwrap.
  3. Enter the source key (for Wrap) or wrapped key (for Unwrap). Select the input representation.
  4. Enter the KEK and its representation, or use Gen KEK to generate an AES key of the selected length (16, 24, or 32 bytes).
  5. Select Run. The result is shown in hexadecimal.

In Wrap mode, the result is the Wrapped Key. In Unwrap mode, the result is the recovered Source key. The up-arrow button moves the result into the source field for another operation. In KW mode, the source key must be at least 16 bytes. KWP supports padding for inputs that do not meet the KW block-size requirement.

docs.title: Key Encapsulation (KEM)
docs.text: KEM uses a public key to generate a shared key and an encapsulated value, then uses the matching private key to recover the same shared key.

docs.title: Encapsulate
docs.text:
1. Open KEM and select Encapsulate.
  2. Choose the public key source: select Use CertMan to select from certificate management, or enable Select private key or public key and provide a certificate or public key file.
  3. Select Encapsulate. The generated shared key and wrapped/encapsulated key are shown as hexadecimal values.

docs.title: Decapsulate
docs.text:
1. Select Decapsulate.
  2. Choose the private key source: Use CertMan, or enable Select private key or public key and provide a private key file.
  3. If the private key file is encrypted, select its encrypted-key option and enter the password.
  4. Enter the encapsulated value in Wrapped Key and select Decapsulate.
  5. The recovered shared key appears in the key output field.

The KEM operation supports RSA, ECDSA, and ML-KEM key types in the current implementation. The key and encapsulated-value fields provide Find, View, Decode, or Type actions for the selected file, where available. Clear buttons remove the corresponding values.

docs.title: Troubleshooting
docs.text:
• Check that the selected representation matches the entered text. Invalid Hex or Base64 input prevents the operation.
  • Key derivation requires a password or secret. HKDF also requires a salt.
  • Key wrapping requires both source data and a KEK. KW requires a source key of at least 16 bytes.
  • KEM encapsulation requires a supported public key or certificate; decapsulation requires the matching supported private key and encapsulated value.
  • Operation failures are reported in a warning, and activity details may also appear in the BerEditor log.

docs.title: KeyPairMan Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Key Pair Management dialog stores, selects, inspects, and uses asymmetric key pairs in BerEditor's KeyPairMan. A key pair is shown with its algorithm, parameter set, and modification time.

Figure 1. KeyPairMan on the List tab. Select a key-pair row to perform an action on that key.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. List / Tools tabs — List manages stored key pairs. Tools works with private keys, public keys, encrypted private keys, private-key information, and certificate signing requests (CSRs).
  2. KeyPair Path — Shows the configured KeyPairMan storage folder. The adjacent filter limits listed key pairs by algorithm or shows All.
  3. Key-pair table — Lists stored pairs by folder name, algorithm, option/parameter, and last-modified time. Select a row before using the action buttons.
  4. Gen KeyPair / Import — Generate a new pair or import key material into KeyPairMan.
  5. View PubKey / View PriKey — Inspect the selected pair's public or private key. Private key material is sensitive.
  6. Decode PubKey / Decode PriKey — Decode the selected key in BerEditor's main window.
  7. Run Encrypt / Run Decrypt / Run Sign / Run Verify — Open the corresponding operation using the selected key material.
  8. Make CSR — Create a certificate signing request using the selected key pair.
  9. Export / Delete / Rename — Export the selected pair, remove it from KeyPairMan, or change its name.
  10. Tools tab controls — Load private/public key files, inspect or decode them, check that a pair matches, create a CSR, save a pair to the list, and encrypt/decrypt a private key. The private-key encryption mode and password are set in this tab.
  11. Save as DER — Select DER output for supported export/save operations in the Tools tab.
  12. OK / Close — OK confirms selection when the dialog is being used to choose a key pair. Close dismisses the manager.

docs.title: Manage Key Pairs
docs.text:
1. Open the List tab and select a row, or choose Gen KeyPair or Import to add key material.
  2. Use View, Decode, or Make CSR to inspect or prepare the selected pair.
  3. Use the Run buttons to launch encryption, decryption, signing, or verification with the selected key.
  4. Use Export, Rename, or Delete as needed. Deleting removes the stored key-pair entry from KeyPairMan.

docs.title: Use the Tools Tab
docs.text:
1. Open Tools and use Find beside the private-key or public-key field to select files. The V, D, and T controls view, decode, or identify key data where available.
  2. Select Check KeyPair to confirm the public and private keys correspond.
  3. Select Make CSR to create a request from the key pair, then inspect or decode the CSR as needed.
  4. Select Save to List to add the pair to KeyPairMan.
  5. To protect or unlock a private key, provide an encrypted private-key file or key, choose an encryption mode and password, then use Encrypt PrivateKey or Decrypt PrivateKey.

docs.title: Tools tab layout
docs.text:
Figure 2. The Tools tab groups key-pair operations, CSR handling, and private-key encryption in one workspace.

The Private Key and Public Key rows each have a Find button and compact controls: C clears the selected path, V opens a view of the key, D decodes its contents in BerEditor, and T identifies the key type. Use Check KeyPair after selecting both inputs to check that the public and private components correspond. Save to List stores the pair in KeyPairMan, while Make CSR creates a certificate signing request from the private key.

The lower fields support related files and operations:

  • Enc PriKey accepts an encrypted private-key file. Use Find to select it, C to clear the path, and D to decode it.
  • PriKey Info is for private-key information data; its C and D controls clear or decode the specified file.
  • CSR displays the CSR path. View opens it for inspection, while C and D clear or decode it.
  • Password is used with the selected encryption mode for private-key encryption or decryption. Encrypt PrivateKey writes an encrypted key, and Decrypt PrivateKey processes an encrypted key using the supplied password.
  • Save as DER selects DER output for supported save/export operations. Leave it unchecked for the other supported output format.
  • Clear All clears the Tools tab inputs so you can start another operation.

The warning at the bottom of the dialog states that private keys stored in KeyPairMan are not encrypted for testing purposes. The password and encryption controls here apply to file-based operations; they do not change that storage behavior. Restrict access to the key-pair directory and use the encryption controls when you need to protect private-key files.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The dialog displays a notice that private keys in KeyPairMan are not encrypted for testing purposes. Protect the storage directory and exported key files accordingly.
  • Run operations require a compatible key type and the appropriate public or private key component.
  • KeyPairMan paths are configured in BerEditor settings; the path shown in the dialog identifies the active store.

docs.title: License Information
docs.text: The License Information dialog displays BerEditor's current license status and provides controls to request, load, update, or remove license information.

docs.title: Message tab
docs.text: The Message tab reports whether BerEditor is licensed. In unlicensed mode, it may show a notice about an expired or missing license. Do stop showing this message for the time being suppresses the notice temporarily; clear it to resume the notices.

docs.title: Current License tab
docs.text:
Field or control Description Email Email associated with the current license. Issued Date License issue date and time. Expire Date License expiration date and time. License Request Opens the license registration page in the system browser. Email / License Key Credentials used when retrieving a license. Get Retrieves and applies a license using the entered email and license key. Use License File Switches to selecting a local license file; the Get button changes to Find. Free License Requests a free license for the entered email address. Update License Updates the current license when the service is available. Remove Removes invalid saved license information after confirmation. Close Closes the dialog.

The available buttons depend on the current license state. For example, Update License is shown for a valid licensed installation, while Free License is offered when no valid license is active.

docs.title: Apply a license
docs.text:
1. To request a license, select License Request and follow the registration page instructions.
  2. Return to BerEditor. Enter the email and license key, then select Get; or enable Use License File and select Find to load a license file.
  3. To request a free license, enter an email address and select Free License, then confirm.
  4. If the license changes successfully, accept the restart prompt to apply it.

Use Update License to renew an existing license when that action is available. Remove is intended for invalid saved license information. Close the dialog when finished.

docs.title: Make BER Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Make BER dialog builds a BER-encoded value from a tag and value. Open it from Tool > Make BER.

Figure 1. Make BER dialog. The header and BER output are updated as the tag settings and value change.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. More Type — Adds additional universal tag types to the Tag type list.
  2. Class — Selects the BER tag class: Universal, Application, Content-Specific, or Private.
  3. Constructed — Sets the constructed bit. SEQUENCE and SET are always constructed; other universal types cannot be changed to constructed in this dialog.
  4. Indefinite — Uses indefinite length for constructed data. This option is enabled only when Constructed is selected. The generated BER ends with the end-of-contents marker 00 00.
  5. Tag / Number — For the Universal class, select a tag type from the list. For the other classes, enter the tag number in hexadecimal. The tag number for Content-Specific is limited to 1F (31) or less in this dialog.
  6. Tag bits — Shows the BER tag byte in binary ([T] 0b).
  7. L — Shows the generated length field in hexadecimal.
  8. Value format and input — Select the input representation and enter the value. Available formats are Hex, String, and Base64. The Len field shows the decoded value length.
  9. C — Clears the value input.
  10. Make Value — Opens a helper for supported value types such as BitString, Integer, or ObjectIdentifier. Availability depends on the selected tag and value format.
  11. BER Header — Displays the generated tag and length bytes in hexadecimal.
  12. BER output — Displays the complete BER value in hexadecimal. Its Len field shows the output length.
  13. Make — Validates and accepts the generated BER value. From Tool > Make BER, the value is then loaded into the main BER view.
  14. Close — Closes the dialog without accepting the generated value.

docs.title: Create a BER Value
docs.text:
1. Open Tool > Make BER.
  2. Choose a Class.
  3. For Universal, choose a tag type. Use More Type if the required universal type is not in the initial list. For another class, enter the tag Number in hexadecimal.
  4. Set Constructed or Indefinite if applicable. These controls are constrained by the selected tag class and type.
  5. Select the value format, then enter the value. The BER Header and BER output update as you edit the settings.
  6. Review the header, length, and complete BER output.
  7. Select Make to validate and load the result into the main BER view.

docs.title: Tag and Value Notes
docs.text:
• The default universal tag is SEQUENCE, with Constructed enabled.
  • NULL has no value input; the value field is disabled for this tag.
  • SEQUENCE and SET require the Constructed bit. Other universal tag types are treated as primitive by this dialog.
  • For a constructed value with Indefinite selected, the BER output uses an indefinite length and appends 00 00 as the end-of-contents marker.
  • A BER BOOLEAN value must be exactly one byte.
  • For BIT STRING, the first value byte must be between 00 and 07, representing the number of unused bits.
  • For non-universal classes, enter the tag number in hexadecimal. The Content-Specific class uses a low tag number up to 1F here.

docs.title: If Validation Fails
docs.text: If the selected input format cannot be decoded, BerEditor reports a format error and returns focus to the value field. Correct the input format or value, then select Make again. Boolean and BitString values have the additional constraints listed above.

docs.title: Make Private Key Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Make Private Key dialog generates asymmetric key pairs and displays their components. It supports RSA, ECC, DSA, and raw-key algorithms, including EdDSA and post-quantum ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA.

Figure 1. Make Private Key dialog with RSA selected. Use the algorithm tabs to view or edit the corresponding key components.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Algorithm — Select the key algorithm: RSA, ECDSA, SM2, DSA, EdDSA, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, or SLH-DSA. The available parameter choices depend on the algorithm.
  2. Parameter — Choose the key size, curve, or algorithm parameter set. For RSA, the default size is 2048 bits. Other algorithms use their respective sizes or named parameter sets.
  3. Exponent — Set the RSA public exponent as a decimal value. The default is 65537; this setting applies to RSA key generation.
  4. PublicKey only — When enabled, the dialog generates or exports only public-key data and disables private-key components where applicable.
  5. RSA tab — Shows RSA public exponent E, primes P and Q, modulus N, private exponent D, CRT exponents DMP1 and DMQ1, and coefficient IQMP. Values are hexadecimal; adjacent fields show their lengths.
  6. ECC tab — Shows the selected curve name and OID, private key, and public point coordinates PubX and PubY.
  7. DSA tab — Shows the domain parameters P, Q, and G, plus the public and private key values.
  8. Raw tab — Select the raw algorithm Name and Param set, then view the raw public and private key values. Raw algorithms include EdDSA, ML-KEM, ML-DSA, and SLH-DSA.
  9. Make — Generates a key pair using the selected algorithm and parameters, then fills the corresponding tab with the generated components.
  10. Decode / Check PublicKey / Check KeyPair — Decode the displayed key in BerEditor, validate the public key, or validate the key pair. These controls use the currently selected key tab.
  11. Save to KeyPairMan — Save the generated key pair to BerEditor's KeyPairMan, when the displayed key data is valid and complete.
  12. Export — Export the key material from the current tab. The PublicKey only setting determines whether public or private key data is selected for export.
  13. Clear All / Close — Clear the key component fields or close the dialog.

docs.title: Generate a Key Pair
docs.text:
1. Select the desired Algorithm.
  2. Choose its Parameter. For RSA, set the key size and decimal Exponent. For ECC, select the curve; for DSA and raw algorithms, select the supported size or parameter set.
  3. Leave PublicKey only unchecked when you need a complete key pair.
  4. Select Make. The generated components appear on the algorithm's tab.
  5. Use Check PublicKey or Check KeyPair to validate the displayed key data.
  6. Select Save to KeyPairMan to store the key pair, or Export to write it in the desired format.

docs.title: Inspect or Export Existing Components
docs.text:
1. Select the tab for the key algorithm.
  2. Enter or review the hexadecimal key components. The displayed length fields update as values change.
  3. Select Decode to open the encoded key in BerEditor's decoder, or use a check button to validate it.
  4. Select Export and choose whether to export public or private key material using PublicKey only.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Private-key fields contain sensitive material. Protect exported private keys and avoid sharing screenshots or logs that reveal key values.
  • RSA exponent input is decimal, while key components on the algorithm tabs are hexadecimal.
  • ECC curve parameters are shown by both curve name and OID. Use matching curve parameters when exchanging or validating ECC key material.
  • The Raw tab is intended for algorithms represented as raw public/private key values; its parameter list changes with the selected raw algorithm.

docs.title: Make TTLV
docs.text: The Make TTLV dialog builds one TTLV item from its tag, type, and value, and displays the resulting encoded message.

docs.title: Fields and controls
docs.text: Control Description Tag Enter a KMIP tag as hexadecimal text. Enter all 6 hex digits for the 3-byte tag. Tag name Shows the recognized name for a known tag. Type Selects the TTLV type, such as Structure, Integer, TextString, or ByteString. Length Displays the value length in bytes as an 8-digit hexadecimal field. Value format Chooses how the value text is interpreted (the available data formats are provided by the application). Value Enter the value in the selected format. Value length Shows the value length in the selected format. TTLV Header Shows the encoded tag, type, and length fields. TTLV Shows the complete encoded item as hexadecimal text, including any required padding. First Set Checkbox shown in the dialog; its behavior is not described here because it is not connected to an action in the current implementation. OK Validates and accepts the constructed item. Cancel Closes the dialog without accepting the item.

docs.title: Create a TTLV item
docs.text:
1. Enter the 6-digit hexadecimal tag. For a recognized KMIP tag, its name appears beside the field.
  2. Choose the TTLV Type.
  3. Choose a value format and enter the value. For a Structure, enter no value or provide a valid TTLV-encoded value.
  4. Review the automatically updated header and complete TTLV output.
  5. Select OK to accept the item.

TTLV values are padded with zero bytes to an 8-byte boundary in the encoded output. The header length reflects the unpadded value length. A tag shorter than 6 digits or invalid Structure content prevents acceptance.

docs.title: OCSP Client Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The OCSP Client creates an Online Certificate Status Protocol request, sends it to a responder, and verifies the returned response. It can include a nonce and optionally sign the request.

Figure 1. OCSP Client dialog. Configure the responder and target certificate, encode or send a request, then verify the response.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. OCSP URL — Enter or select the responder URL. Previously used URLs are retained. Clear clears the URL history/input.
  2. Set OCSP URL from AIA / Set CA from AIA — Read the responder URL or issuer CA certificate from the target certificate's Authority Information Access information.
  3. CA cert — Select the issuer CA certificate. Find browses for a certificate; V, D, and T view, decode, and identify it.
  4. Certificate — Select the certificate whose status is being checked. The dialog can also obtain it from CertMan. The adjacent Find, V, D, and T controls select, view, decode, or identify the certificate.
  5. Use Sign / Use Nonce — Optionally sign the OCSP request with a signing certificate/private key and include a nonce. The signing certificate and key can be selected from CertMan or from individual files; enable Enc PrivateKey and enter its password for a protected key. The nonce value is hexadecimal.
  6. Request — Encode builds the OCSP request. Auto send sends it immediately after encoding; otherwise use Send. C clears the request and D decodes it in BerEditor.
  7. Verify Flags — Enable the flag group and select any applicable response-checking flags: NOCHAIN, NOSIGS, NOINTERN, NOCERTS, NOVERIFY, NOEXPLICIT, NOCASIGN, or NODELEGATED.
  8. Response — Displays the responder response in hexadecimal. View Response opens response details; View CertID inspects the certificate identifier; Verify validates the response. C clears the response and D decodes it.
  9. OCSP Certificate — Select the responder certificate when needed for response verification. Find, V, D, and T select or inspect it.
  10. Clear All / Close — Clear dialog data or close the client.

docs.title: Create and Send a Status Request
docs.text:
1. Enter the OCSP URL or select Set OCSP URL from AIA after choosing a target certificate.
  2. Select the target Certificate. Provide its CA cert or use Set CA from AIA where available.
  3. Optionally enable Use Nonce and enter a hexadecimal nonce. Enable Use Sign and select signing credentials if the responder requires signed requests.
  4. Select Encode. Enable Auto send to transmit immediately, or select Send after reviewing the encoded request.
  5. The response is placed in the Response area when the HTTP request succeeds.

docs.title: Verify a Response
docs.text:
1. Select the relevant responder certificate if needed.
  2. Configure Verify Flags according to the verification requirements.
  3. Select Verify and review the result in BerEditor's message/log area. Use View Response and View CertID to inspect details.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The CA certificate identifies the issuer of the certificate being checked; the OCSP responder certificate is used to verify the signed response. These may be different certificates.
  • Request signing is optional and is separate from the responder's response signature.
  • A successful HTTP send only confirms the responder returned data. Use Verify to validate the OCSP response before relying on its status.

docs.title: PDF Signer Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The PDF Signer signs and verifies PDF documents, adds document security and timestamp information, builds certificate paths, and encrypts or decrypts PDF files.

Figure 1. PDF Signer with the Information tab and Signature controls visible. Use the Verification and Encryption tabs for their respective operations.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. PDF Path / Find — Select the source PDF. Get PDF Information reads document metadata and signature information; C clears the displayed source information.
  2. Source PDF Information tabs — Information lists PDF properties; DSS DocTimeStamp shows document security store and document timestamp details; Path Tree displays certificate-path information. Make Path builds a path for the signing/verification certificate.
  3. Source PDF Password — Enter the password when the source PDF is encrypted.
  4. Signature tab — Set signature labels: Name, Reason, Location, ContactInfo, and Date Time. Enable Use Subject DN to use the certificate subject as the signer name.
  5. Timestamp and DSS options — Enable Use Timestamp and configure TSP to request a signature timestamp. DSS adds validation data; VRI adds per-signature validation-related information when DSS is enabled. DocTimeStamp adds a document timestamp.
  6. Sign / Compress / DSS buttons — Sign creates the PDF signature. Compress controls compression where supported. Add DSS, Add DSS VRI, and Add DocTSP add validation or timestamp data to a PDF.
  7. Verification tab — Configure certificate verification using the certificate, Trust List, CA List, and optional At Time setting. Use Verify Chain and the DSS, VRI, or document-timestamp verification controls to inspect the relevant PDF validation data.
  8. Encryption tab — Use Encrypt or Decrypt for PDF encryption operations. Provide the required passwords and destination as prompted.
  9. Destination PDF / Find / up-arrow — Choose the output PDF path. Find browses for a destination; the up-arrow copies the source path into the destination field.
  10. Clear All / Close — Clear the dialog's paths and information or close it.

docs.title: Sign a PDF
docs.text:
1. Select a source PDF with Find and enter its password if it is encrypted.
  2. Select the signing certificate and private key through CertMan when prompted.
  3. Set the signature labels and date/time. Enable Use Subject DN if the signer name should come from the certificate.
  4. Optionally enable Use Timestamp and configure the TSP. Select DSS, VRI, or DocTimeStamp if the PDF should include validation or timestamp data.
  5. Choose a destination PDF path and select Sign. If the destination already exists, confirm whether to replace it.

docs.title: Verify a PDF Signature
docs.text:
1. Select the signed PDF and enter its password if required.
  2. Review its signature information with Get PDF Information and inspect signer/CMS data as needed.
  3. On the Verification tab, set the certificate and trust options. Use At Time to check against a specific time.
  4. Select Verify for the signature, Verify Chain for certificate-chain validation, and the DSS/VRI or DocTSP verification commands when you need to verify embedded validation/timestamp data.
  5. Review the verification results and certificate path information.

docs.title: Add DSS or Document Timestamp Data
docs.text:
• Select the source PDF and build the certificate path if needed.
  • Use Add DSS to add validation material, Add DSS VRI to add VRI-related material, or Add DocTSP to add a document timestamp.
  • Specify the output PDF destination and inspect the updated information on the DSS DocTimeStamp tab.

docs.title: Encrypt or Decrypt a PDF
docs.text:
1. Select the source PDF and provide its password if it is already encrypted.
  2. Open the Encryption tab and choose Encrypt or Decrypt.
  3. Provide the required credentials and destination path, then run the selected operation.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• PDF signing changes the document and creates a signed output file. Keep the original if you need an unchanged copy.
  • A valid signature does not by itself guarantee that the signer certificate chains to a trusted authority; review signature and chain verification separately.
  • Timestamping depends on the configured TSP service. DSS and VRI features depend on the validation information available for the signing certificate.
  • Protect PDF passwords and signing private keys. Verification results depend on the chosen trust sources and verification time.

docs.title: PKCS7 Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The PKCS7 dialog creates and processes PKCS#7/CMS messages. It supports data and digest containers, signing and signature verification, and enveloped-data encryption and decryption.

Figure 1. PKCS7 dialog in Encode mode. Select Encode or Decode at the top; the available command and controls change with the selected mode.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Encode / Decode — Choose whether to create a PKCS7/CMS message or process an existing one. The source and output labels change to reflect the mode.
  2. Source Data / CMS data — Enter source content or the CMS message. Choose Hex, String, or Base64 for the source representation. Read File loads a file; files can also be dragged into the dialog. In Decode mode, V, D, and T view, decode, and identify the source object. C clears the source.
  3. Select each certificate and private key — Enable this group to select certificate and private-key files directly. Find browses for a file; V, D, and T view details, decode the file in BerEditor, and show its type. Enable Encrypted PrivateKey and enter its password when the private key is password protected.
  4. PKCS7 Flags — Enable the group to apply operation flags. The available flags are NOCERTS, NOSIGS, NOCHAIN, NOINTERN, NOVERIFY, DETACHED, BINARY, and NOATTR. Their effect depends on the selected command.
  5. Verification options — In the certificate verification area, choose whether to validate At Time (using the adjacent date/time), include a selected Certificate, use the CA List, or use the Trust List. These options are used for signature verification; the default screen has Trust List enabled.
  6. Hash and cipher — Select a hash algorithm for signing-related operations and an AES-CBC cipher (aes-128-cbc, aes-192-cbc, or aes-256-cbc) for enveloped-data operations. Controls are enabled when relevant to the selected command.
  7. Command and Auto Detect — Choose an operation. In Decode mode, Auto Detect identifies the CMS type and dispatches to the matching decode/verify operation. Turn it off to choose a decode command manually.
  8. Run button — Executes the selected command. It is labeled Encode or Decode according to the mode.
  9. CMS data / Source data output — Displays the result and its length. The output representation selector and ⬆ transfer button let you reuse the result as input. Export saves the output. V, D, and T view, decode, and identify the output; C clears it. For encoded output, the command name is shown beside the controls.
  10. Clear Data All / Close — Clear the dialog's values or close it.

docs.title: Create a PKCS7/CMS Message
docs.text:
1. Select Encode and enter content in Source Data, or load it with Read File.
  2. Select an encoding command:
  3. Data wraps content in a CMS Data object.
  4. Digest creates a CMS DigestedData object using the selected hash.
  5. Signed creates a signed message. Select the signing certificate and private key.
  6. Enveloped encrypts the content for the selected recipient certificate. Choose an AES-CBC cipher.
  7. Add Signed adds a signer to an existing SignedData message; choose the hash and provide the signing certificate and private key.
  8. Set any applicable flags and options.
  9. Select Encode. The CMS message appears in the output area. Use Export to save it.

docs.title: Decode, Verify, or Decrypt a Message
docs.text:
1. Select Decode and provide the CMS data. Use Read File or drag a file into the dialog if convenient.
  2. Leave Auto Detect enabled to process supported Data, DigestedData, SignedData, or EnvelopedData according to its type. To choose explicitly, turn off Auto Detect and select Verify, Developed, GetData, or GetDigest.
  3. For Verify, configure the certificate and trust/CA/time options as needed. For Developed (decryption of EnvelopedData), select the recipient certificate and matching private key. Enter the private-key password if required.
  4. Select Decode. Extracted data, digest data, verification results, or decrypted content is shown in the output area or reported by the dialog.

docs.title: PKCS7 Flags
docs.text: Flag Purpose NOCERTS Omit signer certificates when creating signed data. NOSIGS Skip signature verification. NOCHAIN Disable certificate-chain verification. NOINTERN Do not search certificates embedded in the message. NOVERIFY Skip signer-certificate verification. DETACHED Create or process detached signed data, where content is separate from the CMS structure. BINARY Treat content as binary data. NOATTR Omit signed attributes when creating signed data.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The available command list depends on Encode or Decode mode. Decode Auto Detect supports CMS Data, DigestedData, SignedData, and EnvelopedData types.
  • Signed and enveloped operations require the appropriate signing or recipient credentials. The certificate and private key must match, and encrypted private-key files require their password.
  • The source representation selector controls how input text is interpreted. The output's T control identifies the CMS type; the displayed output itself is represented using the output format controls.
  • Verification depends on the selected certificate and trust settings. Review the verification result before relying on a signed message.

docs.title: Public-Key Encrypt/Decrypt Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Public-Key Encrypt/Decrypt dialog encrypts data with a public key and decrypts it with the matching private key. It supports RSA, SM2, and ECDSA-based ECIES operations.

Figure 1. Public-Key Encrypt/Decrypt dialog. Choose an operation, provide the data and corresponding key, then run it to view the result.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Input Data — Enter the plaintext to encrypt or ciphertext to decrypt. Select its representation as Hex, String, or Base64. The dialog shows the input length; C clears the input.
  2. Supported algorithms — RSA, SM2, and ECDSA. For ECDSA, this dialog uses ECIES encryption and decryption.
  3. Key source — Use a key managed by KeyPairMan or enable Use CertMan to choose certificate/key material from CertMan. The required key depends on the selected operation.
  4. Select each certificate and private key — Enable this option to specify a certificate or public-key file and a private-key file directly. Use Find to browse for a file. The adjacent V, D, and T controls view information, decode the file in the main BerEditor window, and show the key type, respectively.
  5. Encrypted PrivateKey / Password — Enable this when the selected private-key file is password protected, then enter its password. This applies when reading the private key for decryption.
  6. ECIES parameters — IV, Tag, and the other PublicKey value carry the ECIES parameters. On encryption, the dialog generates these values; on decryption, provide the values associated with the ciphertext. Values are hexadecimal.
  7. Encrypt / Decrypt — Select the operation. Encryption uses a public key; decryption uses the matching private key.
  8. RSA scheme — Choose V15 or OAEP for RSA. This setting does not select an SM2 or ECIES mode.
  9. Encrypt / Decrypt button — Runs the selected operation. The button label follows the selected mode.
  10. Output Data — Displays the result in the selected output representation (Hex, String, or Base64) and shows its length. C clears the result. The up-arrow copies the result into Input Data and sets the input representation to match the output.
  11. Clear Data All — Clears the dialog's data and related values. Close closes the dialog.

docs.title: Encrypt Data
docs.text:
1. Select Encrypt.
  2. Enter the plaintext in Input Data and choose its representation.
  3. Choose the public key or certificate source. If using individual files, enable Select each certificate and private key and select the certificate or public-key file.
  4. For RSA, select V15 or OAEP. For SM2 or ECDSA, use the appropriate public key; RSA scheme selection does not apply.
  5. Select Encrypt. The encrypted result appears in Output Data.
  6. For ECIES, record the generated IV, Tag, and other PublicKey value along with the ciphertext. Decryption requires these parameters.

docs.title: Decrypt Data
docs.text:
1. Select Decrypt.
  2. Enter the ciphertext and choose its representation.
  3. Select the corresponding private key. If it is password protected, enable Encrypted PrivateKey and enter the password.
  4. For RSA, select the same padding scheme used to encrypt the data. For ECIES, enter the associated IV, Tag, and other PublicKey values in hexadecimal.
  5. Select Decrypt. The plaintext appears in Output Data.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Encryption and decryption must use a matching public/private key pair and compatible algorithm parameters.
  • Keep the ECIES parameters with the ciphertext; the ciphertext alone is insufficient for this dialog's ECIES decryption workflow.
  • The output representation controls how the result is displayed, not the cryptographic operation. Use the up-arrow to pass a result back as input.
  • The dialog warns when input data, a required key, or a required password is missing, or when the selected data cannot be decoded in the chosen representation.

docs.title: SCEP Client Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The SCEP Client creates and sends Simple Certificate Enrollment Protocol requests to a CA. It supports certificate Issue, Update, and GetCRL operations, plus retrieval of the CA certificate.

Figure 1. SCEP Client dialog with Issue selected. Use GetCA to retrieve CA certificate information, then create and send the selected request.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. SCEP URL — Enter or select the SCEP endpoint. Clear clears the saved URL list/input.
  2. CA Cert / GetCA — Select a CA certificate with Find, or use GetCA to retrieve the CA certificate from the SCEP server. V, D, and T view, decode, or identify it.
  3. Select each certificate and private key — Enable this group to select client certificate/private-key files directly. Otherwise, use CertMan. Enable Enc PrivateKey and enter the password for an encrypted key.
  4. Sender Nonce / Transaction ID — View or enter the SCEP sender nonce and transaction identifier used to correlate requests and responses.
  5. Command / Make — Choose Issue, Update, or GetCRL, then select Make to build the corresponding request.
  6. Request — Displays the request in hexadecimal. Send transmits it to the SCEP endpoint. C clears and D decodes the request.
  7. Response / Verify — Displays the server response. Verify checks the SCEP response; C clears and D decodes it.
  8. Clear All / Close — Clear dialog data or close the client.

docs.title: Issue a Certificate
docs.text:
1. Enter the SCEP URL and select the CA certificate. Use GetCA if you need to retrieve the CA certificate from the server.
  2. Select Issue and choose Make. The client opens key-pair and CSR dialogs to create enrollment material and prepares the SCEP request.
  3. Select Send to submit the request. Review the response and choose whether to save issued certificate and key material when prompted.

docs.title: Update a Certificate or Retrieve a CRL
docs.text:
1. Enter the SCEP URL and select the CA certificate.
  2. Select Update or GetCRL. Provide the existing certificate and private key when requested.
  3. Select Make, then Send to submit the generated request.
  4. Use Verify to check the response and D to inspect its encoded contents.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Issue creates new key/CSR material as part of request preparation. Update and GetCRL use existing certificate/key context.
  • Keep sender nonce and transaction ID associated with their request/response exchange.
  • Protect private-key passwords and enrollment credentials. Confirm the server response before using newly issued credentials.

docs.title: Settings
docs.text: The Settings dialog controls BerEditor display, parsing, language, and file-related preferences. Some advanced options are available only in the licensed version.

docs.title: Basic tab
docs.text: Setting Description Check for updates automatically Enables automatic update checks when the build supports them. Show only BER selection area Limits the main window to the BER selection area. Show only TTLV selection area Limits the main window to the TTLV selection area. Use log tab at startup Shows the log tab when BerEditor starts. Font Family Selects the monospaced font used by the application. The dialog indicates that a restart is needed. Default Hash Sets the initial hash choice used by applicable cryptographic dialogs. Use CertMan initial check Controls the initial CertMan selection behavior. OCTET STRING and BIT STRING automatic expansion Enables automatic expansion of these BER values in the decode view. PKCS8 PKCS12 encryption method Selects the encryption method used for PKCS#8 and PKCS#12 operations.

docs.title: Advanced tab
docs.text:
Setting Description OID Config File Path to the OID configuration file. Use Find to select a file. File Read Size Size of each read operation when reading a file. Certificate Path Certificate storage path. Find selects a base folder; BerEditor appends its JSPKI subfolder. Language Selects the application language. The setting requires a restart to take effect. Support for changing original keypair Enables support for changing the original key pair. Use fixed hex and bit value area / Characters Sets the fixed width of the hexadecimal and bit-value display area. Automatic online import when creating CA and CRL paths Enables automatic online import during CA and CRL path creation.

Some advanced settings are disabled in unlicensed mode.

docs.title: Apply or restore settings
docs.text:
1. Choose the Basic or Advanced tab and change the required options.
  2. Select OK to save the changes. If you changed the language, accept the restart prompt to apply it.
  3. Select Cancel to discard edits in the dialog.
  4. Select Restore defaults to clear saved settings. Confirm the prompt; BerEditor may offer to restart.

docs.title: Signature / Verify Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Signature / Verify dialog creates or verifies an asymmetric digital signature using input data or a file. Open it from Cryptography > Sign/Verify.

Figure 1. Signature / Verify dialog. Select the data, signing key or verification certificate, algorithm options, and operation.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Use KeyPairMan key / Use CertMan — Select the key source used when the individual certificate/private-key file group is not enabled. The selected manager provides the required key or certificate.
  2. Input Data / Input File — Enter message data directly or select a file to sign or verify.
  3. Input Type / Input area — Select the representation (such as Hex, String, or Base64), enter the data, and review the calculated length. In file mode, use Find and monitor file information and progress.
  4. Init / Update / Final / Reset — Perform signing or verification incrementally. Initialize with the chosen key, feed data blocks with Update, and complete the operation with Final.
  5. Select each certificate and private key — Enable this group to select the key material from files rather than a key manager.
  6. Cert or PubKey — Select a certificate or public key for verification. Find selects the file; V opens its details; D decodes it in BerEditor; T reports its key type.
  7. PrivateKey — Select the private key for signing. Find, V, D, and T provide file selection, details, BER decoding, and key-type information.
  8. Encrypted PrivateKey / Password — Select this when the private-key file is encrypted, then enter its password.
  9. Hash — Select a hash for RSA, ECDSA, DSA, and SM2 signatures. SM2 requires SM3.
  10. RSA Signature schemes — Select the RSA signature scheme, such as V15 or PSS, when signing or verifying with RSA.
  11. Sign / Verify — Select the operation. The run button changes to Sign or Verify.
  12. SignDigest — Signs or verifies an already-computed digest. The input must have the selected hash's digest length; the dialog warns if the lengths differ.
  13. Signature — Displays the generated signature in Hex when signing. For verification, enter the expected signature here as hexadecimal. The length is shown beside it.
  14. Clear Data All / Close — Clears input, key paths, signature and status, or closes the dialog.

docs.title: Sign a Message
docs.text:
1. Select Input Data or Input File and provide the message.
  2. Select Sign.
  3. Choose a private key source:
  4. Use KeyPairMan key or CertMan from the top controls; or
  5. Enable Select each certificate and private key, then select a private key file. If it is encrypted, enable Encrypted PrivateKey and enter its password.
  6. Select the hash algorithm. For RSA, choose the RSA signature scheme as appropriate.
  7. Select Sign. The signature is displayed in hexadecimal.

docs.title: Verify a Signature
docs.text:
1. Provide the same message data or file that was signed.
  2. Select Verify.
  3. Choose the public key source: a certificate or public key from the key manager, CertMan, or the file selection group.
  4. Choose the matching hash and RSA signature scheme.
  5. Enter the expected signature in the Signature field as hexadecimal.
  6. Select Verify and read the success or failure message.

docs.title: Sign or Verify a Digest
docs.text: Select SignDigest to operate directly on a precomputed digest rather than hashing a message through the normal Sign/Verify path. Enter the digest in the input area using the selected input representation. The dialog checks its length against the selected hash and asks whether to continue if they differ.

docs.title: Incremental Operations and Notes
docs.text:
• Use Init, Update, and Final to process data in stages. Select Reset before starting another staged operation.
  • The same message bytes, key pair, hash, and RSA signature scheme must be used for successful verification.
  • SM2 uses SM3. If another hash is selected, BerEditor prompts to switch to SM3.
  • Some key algorithms do not support the staged Init/Update/Final workflow. Use the one-shot Sign or Verify action when prompted.

docs.title: SSL Check Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The SSL Check dialog connects to an HTTPS server and reports TLS, certificate, and trust information. It can also test servers that require mutual TLS client authentication.

Figure 1. SSL Check dialog on the Server tab. Enter a server URL and select Check to test the TLS connection and certificate chain.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Server / Mutual tabs — Configure ordinary server checks on Server. Use Mutual to configure a client certificate and private key for mutual TLS.
  2. View Trust List / Use Mutual Auth — Open CertMan's trusted root list or enable client-certificate authentication.
  3. Protocol options — Check NO_SSLv3, NO_TLSv1, NO_TLSv1_1, NO_TLSv1_2, and NO_TLSv1_3 to disable the corresponding protocol versions for the test connection.
  4. Check Host Name — Enable hostname verification so the server certificate is checked against the requested host.
  5. Verify Mode / Verify Depth — Set the TLS certificate verification mode and maximum chain depth. The displayed default depth is 4.
  6. Trust CA — Optionally select a trusted CA certificate file with Find. V, D, and T view, decode, and identify the selected file.
  7. Fix Cipher — Enable a restricted cipher configuration, choose a TLS version and cipher, and select Add. Clear removes the configured cipher selection.
  8. URL / Check — Enter a hostname or URL and select Check. If no scheme is supplied, the dialog assumes https://; the default port is 443. C clears the URL field.
  9. Results table — Lists tested URL, port, certificate distinguished name, and expiry. Select or right-click a row for available certificate actions, including viewing, decoding, or checking it again.
  10. Clear URLs / Refresh — Clear the current result list or rerun checks for the saved URLs.
  11. SSL Tree and Log — Tree displays certificate authority/path information; Log shows connection and verification details. Clear Result clears results; Clear Log clears the log.
  12. Show Information / Close — Opens the selected server's SSL information window or closes the dialog.

docs.title: Check an HTTPS Server
docs.text:
1. On the Server tab, configure protocol versions, hostname checking, verification mode, and verification depth as needed.
  2. Optionally select a Trust CA certificate or use the configured trust list.
  3. Enter a URL such as https://example.com, or a hostname such as example.com.
  4. Select Check. Review the result table, certificate tree, and log for connection and chain status.
  5. Select Show Information to inspect details for the selected result. Use Refresh to check saved URLs again.

docs.title: Check a Mutual TLS Server
docs.text:
1. Enable Use Mutual Auth and open the Mutual tab.
  2. Provide the client CA certificate and select a client certificate/private-key pair, either from CertMan or with the individual certificate and private-key file controls.
  3. If the private key is encrypted, enable Encrypted PrivateKey and enter its password.
  4. Return to the server check and select Check. The client credentials are presented during the TLS handshake.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The URL check tests the live server connection using the current network, TLS, hostname, and trust settings. A server's configuration and certificate status can change over time.
  • Disabling protocol versions or restricting ciphers changes the handshake options and may prevent connection to servers that do not support the remaining choices.
  • Mutual TLS requires a client certificate and its matching private key. Keep private-key files and passwords confidential.
  • A successful TLS connection and certificate verification are distinct from application-level security or the server's identity beyond the selected verification checks.

docs.title: Shamir Secret Sharing Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Shamir Secret Sharing [GF(256)] dialog splits a secret into shares and reconstructs it from a threshold number of shares. Use the same prime value and threshold settings when splitting and joining.

Figure 1. Shamir Secret Sharing dialog. The upper section splits a source value into shares; the lower section combines selected shares to reconstruct the value.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Shares — Number of shares to create. The default is 5.
  2. Threshold — Minimum number of shares required to reconstruct the secret. The default is 3.
  3. Prime — Prime value used by the sharing operation, entered as hexadecimal. The selected Bytes value sets the size for Make Prime; available choices are 8, 16, 32, 64, 128, and 256 bytes. C clears the prime. IsPrime checks whether the entered value is prime.
  4. Source — Secret value to split. Select its input representation (Hex, String, or Base64), enter the value, and select Split. C clears the source; the adjacent field shows its length.
  5. Shared — Enter a share value in hexadecimal and select Add to append it to the share list. The adjacent field displays its length.
  6. Shared value list — Shows the shares available for reconstruction. Right-click a row to copy or delete it. Clear removes all listed shares.
  7. Join — Reconstructs the original secret from the listed shares using the configured threshold and prime.
  8. Joined — Displays the reconstructed value using the selected representation (Hex, String, or Base64). C clears the result; the adjacent field shows its length.
  9. Clear Data All / Close — Clears the values and share list, or closes the dialog.

docs.title: Split a Secret
docs.text:
1. Set Shares to the total number of shares to generate and Threshold to the minimum number needed to reconstruct the secret.
  2. Enter a prime in Prime, or choose a byte size and select Make Prime. Use IsPrime to check a manually entered value.
  3. Enter the secret in Source and select its representation.
  4. Select Split. The generated share values appear in the list. Save or copy the shares and keep the threshold and prime information available for reconstruction.

docs.title: Join Shares
docs.text:
1. Enter the same Prime and Threshold used for splitting.
  2. Add share values to the Shared field one at a time, selecting Add after each. Shares must be hexadecimal values.
  3. Add at least the threshold number of shares, then select Join.
  4. Read the reconstructed secret in Joined and choose the desired output representation.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The prime must be greater than the source value. An insufficient prime causes the split operation to fail.
  • Reconstruction requires at least the configured threshold number of shares; the dialog also requires at least two shares in the list.
  • Duplicate shares are rejected when adding them. Use the share list's right-click menu to copy or remove a share.
  • Shares and the original secret are sensitive. Store shares separately and clear the dialog when finished.

docs.title: Text View Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Text View dialog presents decoded BER or KMIP TTLV data as an indented text listing, or shows its hexadecimal values. Open it from Tool > Text View.

Figure 1. Text View dialog. String View is selected by default; choose Hex View to inspect encoded bytes.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Find — Loads a binary file to view. BerEditor parses it as BER or, when detected, KMIP TTLV.
  2. String View — Displays parsed fields and values in an indented text layout. This is the default view.
  3. Hex View — Displays parsed structures and their hexadecimal bytes.
  4. View Information — Adds an ASCII/printable-text column in Hex View. This option is available only in Hex View and is disabled for String View.
  5. Output area — Shows the listing. It is read-only and does not wrap long lines.
  6. Print / Print Preview — Prints the displayed listing or previews it before printing.
  7. Close — Closes the dialog.

docs.title: View Data
docs.text:
1. Open Text View from the selected data in BerEditor, or select Find to load a file.
  2. Choose String View or Hex View.
  3. In Hex View, optionally select View Information to show printable characters alongside hexadecimal bytes.
  4. Scroll through the parsed output. Use Print or Print Preview if needed.

The viewer detects KMIP TTLV data and displays its parsed structure. Otherwise, it parses the input as BER. You can also drag and drop a local file onto the dialog.

docs.title: View Modes
docs.text:
• String View focuses on decoded values and structure. The information-column option is unavailable in this mode.
  • Hex View shows bytes in groups of up to 16, with offsets and structural indentation. Enable View Information to include printable text beside the bytes.
  • The view area is read-only; use the main BerEditor tools to edit or construct data.

docs.title: TSP Client Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The TSP Client creates Time-Stamp Protocol requests, sends them to a timestamp authority, and verifies the returned timestamp token and signature.

Figure 1. TSP Client dialog. Hash the data, create and send a timestamp request, then verify the token returned by the TSA.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. TSP URL — Enter or select the timestamp authority URL. Clear clears the URL list/input.
  2. Policy — Optionally enter the requested timestamp policy OID.
  3. Input — Enter the data to timestamp and select its representation (Hex, String, or Base64). The adjacent field shows its length.
  4. Hash / Make — Choose a hash algorithm and select Make to calculate the digest of the input. The digest appears beside the button.
  5. Request — Encode creates a TSP request using the input, selected hash, optional policy, and nonce setting. C clears the request; D decodes it.
  6. TSP Server requires authorization — Enable this group and enter the server's Username and Password for HTTP Basic authentication.
  7. Use Nonce / Auto send / Send — Include a nonce in the request, transmit automatically after encoding, or send the current request manually.
  8. Certificate included in verification — Configure At Time, Certificate, CA List, and Trust List for response verification. The default screen has Trust List enabled.
  9. Response — Displays the timestamp response in hexadecimal. TST Information displays the parsed timestamp information; View CMS inspects the CMS token; Verify validates the response; VerifySigned checks the signed token. C clears and D decodes the response.
  10. Clear All / Close — Clear dialog data or close the client.

docs.title: Request a Timestamp
docs.text:
1. Enter the source data in Input and choose its representation.
  2. Select a Hash and choose Make to compute the digest. The request is built from the data and selected hash.
  3. Optionally enter a Policy OID, enable Use Nonce, and provide server credentials if authorization is required.
  4. Select Encode. Enable Auto send to transmit immediately, or choose Send manually.
  5. Review the returned response in the Response area.

docs.title: Verify the Timestamp
docs.text:
1. Select the certificate verification options: Trust List, CA List, an optional Certificate, and At Time if checking at a specific date/time.
  2. Select Verify to validate the timestamp response and VerifySigned to verify the signed token as needed.
  3. Use TST Information or View CMS to inspect the token contents.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• The source data's digest is sent in the request; the original data itself is not included in a standard timestamp request.
  • The selected hash and policy must be supported by the timestamp authority.
  • Successful transmission does not establish that a token is valid. Review the verification result and trust settings.

docs.title: TTLV Client
docs.text: The TTLV Client sends a hexadecimal KMIP TTLV request to a server and displays the hexadecimal response.

docs.title: Connection and TLS fields
docs.text:
Control Description KMIP URL Server address. Previously used URLs are available in the editable list. Clear (URL) Clears the saved URL history and the current URL entry. CA Cert CA certificate used to verify the server for TLS. Find selects a certificate file. The adjacent V, D, and T controls view, decode, or identify the certificate. Client certificate and private key Optional client identity fields. Enable the certificate/key group to select files directly; otherwise the client can prompt you to select them from CertMan. Encrypted PrivateKey / Password Enable this option and enter the password when the selected client private key is encrypted.

For https or ssl URLs, the client establishes TLS and uses the CA certificate. Client certificate and private key selection supports mutual TLS when required by the server. For other URL schemes, it uses a plain socket connection.

docs.title: Request and response
docs.text: Control Description Request Hexadecimal TTLV bytes to send. The length is displayed with the request. C / D (Request) Clear the request / decode it in the main BerEditor view. TTLV Encoder Opens the request encoder and places an accepted encoded request here. Read Main Copies TTLV data from the main BerEditor window into the request field. Auto send Sends a request immediately after accepting it from TTLV Encoder. Send Connects to the configured server and sends the request. The response is placed in the Response field. Response Hexadecimal TTLV response returned by the server. C / D (Response) Clear the response / decode it in the main BerEditor view. Clear All Clears request and response data. Close Closes the client dialog.

docs.title: Send a request
docs.text:
1. Enter or select a KMIP URL.
  2. For TLS, select the CA Cert. If the server requests a client identity, select a certificate and private key, or choose them through CertMan. Provide the private-key password if needed.
  3. Enter a hexadecimal TTLV request, select Read Main to reuse the main-window TTLV data, or use TTLV Encoder to create a request.
  4. Select Send. With Auto send enabled, a request created through TTLV Encoder is sent as soon as it is accepted.
  5. Review the hexadecimal response. Select D to decode a request or response in the main window.

The application saves successfully used URLs in the URL history. Ensure the URL, certificates, and request are appropriate for the KMIP server before sending.

docs.title: TTLV Encoder
docs.text: The TTLV Encoder creates a KMIP request by selecting an operation and filling its parameters. The output is a hexadecimal TTLV message.

docs.title: Authentication
docs.text: The Authentication group is optional. Enable it to include a KMIP UserID and Password in the request.

docs.title: Request parameters
docs.text:
Available parameters depend on the selected operation. The dialog enables the relevant fields.

Field Purpose UUID Object unique identifier used by operations that target an existing object. Length Length parameter, used by applicable operations such as random number retrieval. Hash Hash or signature digest selection. The initial selection follows BerEditor's default hash setting. Attribute Attribute used by attribute operations. ObjectType Object category such as SecretKey, PrivateKey, PublicKey, or Certificate. Mode Cryptographic mode, including RSA modes and AES modes where applicable. Algorithm RSA, ECDSA, or AES. KeyLength / Option Key size or algorithm-specific option. ECDSA options include P-256, P-384, and P-521; AES sizes are 16, 24, and 32 bytes. IV format / IV Input format and initialization vector for operations that use an IV. Input format / Input Data for the selected operation. Choose Hex, String, or Base64; Find loads data from a file. Signature Signature bytes used by Verify.

docs.title: Select an operation
docs.text:
The Type selector groups commands:

  • Object: Create, Activate, Get, Destroy, Register, Locate, Create Key Pair.
  • Cryptography: Encrypt, Decrypt, Sign, Verify, Hash, RNG Seed, RNG Retrieve.
  • Attribute: Add Attribute, Get Attributes, Modify Attribute, Get Attribute List, Delete Attribute.

Choose the group and then the command. Fill the fields that become available for that operation. For example, Encrypt and Decrypt use an object UUID and input; Verify also needs a signature; RNG Retrieve uses a length.

docs.title: Generate and use output
docs.text:
1. Select a Type and command.
  2. Enter the operation parameters. Enable Authentication and provide credentials if the request requires them.
  3. Select Encode. The generated TTLV appears in Output as hexadecimal text.
  4. Use the output decode control to inspect the encoded request in BerEditor's main view. Use Clear controls to clear individual input, signature, or output areas; Clear All resets the form.
  5. Select OK to return the generated output when that button is available. In managed mode, the dialog is used as an encoder panel and OK is hidden. Close exits the dialog.

docs.title: VID Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The VID dialog creates and verifies a VID (Virtual ID) using an identity value, a random value, and a selected hash algorithm. It also displays the associated hash content for inspection.

Figure 1. VID dialog. Enter the same identity and random value used to create a VID, then generate or verify the value.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. SSN — Enter the identity value used in the VID calculation. The adjacent field displays its length.
  2. Random — Enter the random value and select its representation (Hex, String, or Base64). The adjacent field displays the decoded length.
  3. VID — Displays the VID as hexadecimal. D decodes the value in BerEditor's main window; C clears it. The adjacent field shows the length.
  4. Hash — Select the hash algorithm used when creating a VID. The initial value follows BerEditor's configured default hash.
  5. Make VID / Verify VID — Generate a VID and its hash content, or verify the entered VID against the supplied identity and random value.
  6. Hash Content — Displays the hexadecimal hash content produced during generation or recovered during successful verification. D decodes it in BerEditor; C clears it. The adjacent field shows the length.
  7. Clear All / Close — Clear the SSN, random value, VID, and hash content, or close the dialog.

docs.title: Create a VID
docs.text:
1. Enter the identity value in SSN.
  2. Enter the random value and select its representation.
  3. Choose the Hash algorithm.
  4. Select Make VID. The generated VID and corresponding Hash Content appear in their fields.

docs.title: Verify a VID
docs.text:
1. Enter the same identity value and random value used to create the VID. Select the correct random-value representation.
  2. Enter the VID in hexadecimal in the VID field.
  3. Select Verify VID. A successful verification displays the recovered Hash Content and reports the result in BerEditor's message/log area.

docs.title: Notes
docs.text:
• Verification requires the original identity value and random value, with the same random-value encoding used when the VID was created.
  • The VID field and Hash Content field use hexadecimal values. Use their D buttons to inspect the encoded data in BerEditor.
  • The dialog records the identity value, random value, hash, hash content, and VID in BerEditor's log during generation. Consider this when handling identifying or sensitive input.

docs.title: X.509 Compare
docs.text: The X509 Compare dialog compares two X.509 objects and displays corresponding fields side by side. It supports certificates, certificate revocation lists (CRLs), and certificate signing requests (CSRs).

docs.title: Select inputs
docs.text:
Control Description Comparison target Select Certificate, CRL, or CSR. A Path / B Path Paths to the two input files. You can use Find or drop files onto the dialog; dropped files fill A first and then B. Find Selects an input file matching the chosen comparison type. V Opens the selected object in its detail viewer. D Decodes the selected file in the main BerEditor view. Auto detection X509 type Detects the input object types automatically and disables manual type selection. Compare Compares the two inputs and populates the results table. Result indicator Shows whether the objects are the same or different, or that comparison has not yet run.

The comparison table contains a field name and the values from A and B. Difference indicators mark fields whose values differ. Double-clicking a value opens the corresponding certificate, CRL, or CSR details.

docs.title: Inspect field values
docs.text: Select a row to show its detailed A and B values in the X509 A and B Value panel. Use Show Value if the panel is hidden. BER Compare compares the encoded BER data for the selected objects in BerEditor's BER comparison view.

docs.title: Compare two objects
docs.text:
1. Choose the comparison target, or enable automatic X.509 type detection.
  2. Select the A and B files with Find, or drag and drop them into the dialog. Confirm both paths are populated.
  3. Select Compare.
  4. Review the overall result and compare corresponding fields in the table. Select a row to inspect its detailed values, or double-click a value to open the object's information dialog.
  5. Select BER Compare to inspect the encoded structures. Use Clear to remove both inputs and results, and Close when finished.

A and B must contain the same X.509 object type. BerEditor reports a warning if a file cannot be recognized or the selected inputs have different types.

docs.title: Data Converter Dialog Guide
docs.text:
The Data Converter converts data between text and common encoded representations. Open it from Tool > Data Converter.

Figure 1. Data Converter dialog layout. This is an illustrative diagram based on the UI definition, not a screenshot of the running application.

docs.title: Screen Areas
docs.text:
1. Read File — Loads a file into the input area as hexadecimal data.
  2. Input format and input area — Choose the format of the source data and enter or paste its value.
  3. Input Len — Shows the length calculated using the selected input format.
  4. Conversion — Converts the source bytes to the selected output format.
  5. Conversion Format — Selects the output representation. Show printable text is available when String is selected.
  6. Export — Opens the export dialog for the converted bytes.
  7. Up arrow — Moves the output into the input area and sets the input format to the selected output format.
  8. Output / Hex Dump tabs — Show the converted text or a hexadecimal dump of its bytes.
  9. Clear / Close — Clear input or output content, or close the dialog.

docs.title: Dialog Controls
docs.text: Control Description Read File Loads a file into the input area as hexadecimal data. Files larger than 1 MB are rejected. Input format Select how BerEditor should interpret the input: Hex, String, Base64, URL, or Base64URL. Input area Enter or paste the source data.
